Have you ever met an intelligent creationist? I've met intelligent creationists, but never any creationists in person who actually understood evolution. Every time I talked to an intelligent creationist about how they thought evolution worked, I invariably found that they didn't actually understand. Their views tend to be a mish-mash of Lamarckism, teleological thinking, evolution being progression towards a goal, and human exceptionalism, along with a lack of knowledge of how evolution works, and even a lack of knowledge of modern day organisms. These types of misconceptions drive such questions as wondering why there are still monkeys if we evolved from monkeys (though it's never why there are still birds if penguins evolved from birds), or wondering whether the first fish to crawl onto land would have had either gills or lungs (totally ignoring all the existing fish that have both). You can browse through the Index to Creationist Claims to get an idea of the types of arguments creationists might use. I don't wholly blame these folks, either. They were raised in an environment where creationism was the default, from their parents to their preachers, to possibly even their school teachers (my daughter's high school biology teacher made an announcement at the start of the lesson on evolution that, as a Christian, she didn't believe in it, herself, but it was just part of the curriculum that they had to get through). They were taught all these misleading creationist arguments from people they trusted from a very young age. So the smartest kids were actually the best at absorbing those lessons. And since it takes a while for people to fully develop critical thinking skills, and a fair amount of discipline to go back and apply that to things you think you already know, it's hardly a surprise that those bright kids brought up within a creationist environment carried that belief into their adulthood. (And to be fair, ask yourself how you know that matter is composed of atoms and that atoms are composed of even smaller particles – do you really understand the evidence, or is it just common knowledge that you were taught back when you were younger?) I will say, though, that the number of intelligent, well-educated creationists I've met is rather small. You can definitely see a correlation vs. education level (note that graph is a bit old from 2005): SOURCE: Americans Weigh In on Evolution vs. Creationism in Schools So yes, I've met otherwise intelligent folks who were also creationists. But once you talk with them, it almost invariably turns out that, for whatever reason, they don't actually understand evolution. I have yet to meet a single person in real life who could accurately explain evolution yet still rejected it.

What is the reasoning behind atheists thinking it's illogical to believe in god? Should people be allowed to have their own beliefs without being challenged by others? Let's take your latter two questions first: Should people be allowed to have their own beliefs... Yes without being challenged by others? Absolutely not. This is the type of delicate little snowflake mentality that so many people complain about. All beliefs should be robust enough that they can withstand inspection. If they're not, then maybe they weren't such good beliefs in the first place. Now, I'm not saying life needs to be one continuous debate during all waking hours. There's a time and place for everything, and there's a difference between debate and badgering (or to make a verb of a different animal, sea lioning). But yes, you should at least occasionally have discussions with people who disagree with you about challenging topics – politics, religion, morality, pineapple on pizza, etc. If you never challenge yourself, you'll never grow. And if you limit yourself to echo chambers of only like minded people, you'll never truly understand the wider world and why different people do things differently from you. I can think of plenty of examples from my own life where I'm grateful to the people who challenged me and helped me to see things differently. As far as your first question, well, that could be an entire book. But the short of it is, all the evidence we do have for God and Christianity is best explained as a mythology that developed out of previous mythologies. Heck, we even have evidence of Yahweh's origins in the Canaanite pantheon as a storm god – NOT the one and only God and creator of the universe. Other religions and their holy books are largely similar in that they've developed over generations as mythology. And the other big, glaring problem that they all have is a complete lack of credible evidence. Oh sure, Hindus, Buddhists, Christians, and Muslims all get warm fuzzy feelings when they pray, and some even manage to convince themselves that unlikely events and coincidences are evidence of their particular god(s) (but obviously, not the other gods). But this evidence hardly ever seems credible to outsiders who don't already share their beliefs. So there you go. We think it's not reasonable to believe in gods in general because there's no good evidence, and the capital G God in particular because the evidence we do have shows that he's a product of human myth making. And while we all certainly have a right to hold any beliefs we want, we should also be open to being challenged about those beliefs. That's the only way we grow as individuals.

If you don’t reach escape velocity, but with as much fuel as you need, would you be able to leave Earth? There are a several things to understand here. First is what escape velocity actually means. It's the velocity you would have to be moving, that without any more thrust (i.e. just coasting from then on out) that you would be on a path to eventually 'escape' Earth's gravity (or whatever other body you're talking about escaping, such as the Sun, the Moon, or other planets). Next, escape velocity is dependent on your distance from the Earth (or whatever other body), since the influence of Earth's gravity decreases the further away you get. At the surface, escape velocity is 25k mph (40k km/h). But as you get further away from Earth, the escape velocity drops pretty rapidly at first, and then slowly begins approaching zero. But another big consideration is something known as the sphere of influence (or the related Hill sphere). While it's technically true that gravity from the Earth extends to an infinite distance, there are so many other bodies in our own solar system and broader universe, that at a relatively 'minor' distance (in astronomical terms, at least), the Earth's gravity becomes negligible compared to other bodies. Within our solar system, for example, the Earth's sphere of influence (per Wikipedia) is 577k miles (929k km), which is roughly 2.4x further away than the Moon orbits the Earth. Once you get further than that from the Earth, the Sun's gravity will overwhelm the Earth's, and an object's motion will be governed almost entirely by the Sun's gravity (assuming it's not within some other planet or moon's sphere of influence). So, if you were thinking of escape velocity as 25k mph, realize that that's only close to the surface of the Earth. If you had some means to continuously provide thrust and continuously move away from Earth, eventually you would get far enough away that whatever speed you were moving would be greater than the Earth's escape velocity at that distance – it will just be a lot lower than that 25k mph at the surface. Or, if you were to travel far enough that you went past the Earth's sphere of influence, then the Earth's gravity would be negligible compared to the Sun's, and your path would instead be dominated by the Sun's gravity. (And of course, if you could somehow keep moving away from the Sun, you would eventually get far enough away that the Sun's gravity would be negligible compared to the overall galaxy.) The kicker, though, is how you would actually accomplish that continuous thrust, and just exactly what you mean by "with as much fuel as you need". Rockets already are designed to get the most bang for the buck out of the fuel they can carry. They accelerate so quickly because it is the best way to do it. Consider the extreme – imagine if you had a rocket that generated just enough thrust to hover*. You'd sit there burning fuel, but not climbing. You'd eventually run out of fuel without going anywhere, no matter how much fuel you carried. If you barely increased your thrust, you'd climb slowly, but you'd still run out of fuel before you made it very far. And it's not simply a matter of carrying more fuel. That extra fuel is going to make you heavier, which means you'll need even more thrust, burning more fuel, in a vicious cycle of diminishing returns. You really need to read up on the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation if you want to understand this mathematically, but the best use of your fuel is to accelerate as quickly as possible. As long as we're stuck using rockets, slow, leisurely climbs just aren't a realistic possibility to get into space. *Of course, this thought experiment is still simplifying things, since your rocket will get lighter as it burns off fuel. But I suppose you could be using rocket engines that could be throttled, so that you can constantly adjust the thrust to that required for hover.

How did first eye evolve? Where did all the parts come from and how did those parts ”knew” to combine so as to form an eye? Eyes are a great example of how evolution works by small, incremental changes that offer benefits at each stage*. And there are actually plenty of living animals that have preserved many of these stages, so it's not mere conjecture or just-so stories that these stages could have been useful. We see animals actually making use of these different types of eyes throughout nature. The most primitive 'eyes' I know of personally are those of hydras, tiny freshwater predators that normally attach themselves to something stationary and catch passing prey with their tentacles. They don't even have brains, but just a sort of nerve net. Their proto-eyes are little more than light sensitive individual neurons located throughout their bodies. But even these simple photoreceptors are enough to induce specific day-time and night-time behaviors, modulate the way they discharge their stinging cells, and guide them towards light sources when they do actually move. ABOVE: Anatomy of a hydra. Some of those 'sensory neurons' are photosensitive. Although not shown in this particular figure, such photosensitive neurons are more common in the tentacles in conjunction with the stinging cells. SOURCE: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.12.14.422784v1.full Moving on, let's focus on just molluscs. Here are various eyes known from living molluscs: The first is simply a patch of light sensitive cells, and can be found in limpets. It can't distinguish direction, but having an entire organ dedicated to light detection is a bit more sophisticated and sensitive than the individual neurons of the hydra. Next comes the cup eye, such as is found in abalone. This eye still can't form an image (there's no way to focus the light), but it does provide more information about the direction the light is coming from, so it still offers an advantage over the limpet's eye patch. It shouldn't be hard to imagine how a cup eye could gradually develop a more pronounced recess to enable even better direction discrimination. But if you keep carrying on that process, you'll eventually end up with a recess so pronounced that you actually can start to form an image. And so, you end up with a pinhole eye like that found in a nautilus. And from the pinhole eye of the nautilus, it's not hard to imagine the benefit of fully enclosing that eye with a transparent membrane (to keep out debris and keep the pinhole itself from getting clogged), and then for that membrane to gradually take on the role of a lens to better focus the image, and allow the opening to be bigger to gather even more light, such as the primitive lens in a marine snail. And from there, it's just more gradual evolution and improvements until you end up with a full, complex camera type eye of an octopus or a squid. So, to address the wording of your question, the 'parts' came from gradual evolution over many generations, as mutations incrementally improved the functionality of what was originally just light sensitive neurons. And of course, the parts didn't 'know' anything about the process. That's the whole point of the theory of natural selection. The organisms that acquired those traits, purely by chance, just happened to have more success in reproduction than their relatives who didn't. But, since these mutations are random, and can only be inherited by descendants of the individuals in which they first appear, not every lineage is necessarily going to acquire these mutations. And if an animal occupies an ecological niche where vision isn't all that important, then not having these more advanced eyes isn't going to be much of a detriment, anyway. So, while some lineages did evolve more complex eyes, various other lineages have gone on maintaining more primitive versions of the organ. But this still goes to show that those more primitive versions are indeed useful. Note: Portions of this answer adapted from my previous answer: *That introduction was simplifying things a bit. Evolutionary changes don’t necessarily have to be beneficial at each stage. They can also be neutral or nearly neutral, as in the case of genetic drift. But the main point is that organisms must be fully functional and adapted to their environment in every generation. You don’t get mutations in anticipation of future benefit.

For those who experienced the eclipse today, what are your thoughts? I've seen a few sources overhyping eclipses a bit, so I don't want to oversell it, but it was very, very cool. Living about 2 hrs outside the path of totality myself, it was definitely worth the trip to get myself into a location to see the total eclipse, since a total solar eclipse really is an altogether different experience than a partial solar eclipse. Since my wife is working a contract away from home right now and got a few days off, we decided to make an event of it. We both arrived in Ft. Worth the day before, and spent the day going to a small wine tasting festival and then a night out in downtown Ft. Worth (hat tip to The Flying Saucer). The next morning, the day of the eclipse, we drove down to Mansfield, a small town on the outskirts of the DFW metro area, since that's where most of my wife's family lives. There's nothing like last minute planning, so an hour before the eclipse was forecast to start, we were at Walmart buying hotdogs, hamburgers, and other supplies for a cookout, while my sister in law was scrambling to clean up her house. I did plan enough ahead to have my telescope ready to go, along with a sun funnel that I threw together on Saturday. I got that set up in her driveway as family members began rolling in, so we were able to track the eclipse with that, while everybody had their own eclipse glasses, too. Our eclipse watching group included a few of us who had the day off, one person who called in to take the day off, and a few nieces and nephews skipping the school day (worth it). ABOVE: The start of the eclipse through my telescope – note that this setup lets you see the sunspots, which you don't notice through eclipse glasses. Our biggest stressor was the weather. The forecast was for a cloudy day, and the day of did turn out to be partly cloudy. Throughout the time that the eclipse was occurring, we'd have clouds periodically roll in and block our view. There was one particularly big one that rolled into place as totality was getting close. Google told me that totality was supposed to start at 1:39 in Dallas, and I don't think that cloud blew out of the way until 1:36. So it cleared out just in time. Though I do feel sorry for the people downwind of us who had that cloud blow in just in time to block their view. When the sun was completely blocked by the moon, it really was awesome. I haven't seen many photos that do justice to what it looks like with your own eyes. This photo below is about as close as I've seen, though it was from a previous eclipse back in 2010. Per the description at the site where I found this, it's a composite image composed of short, medium, and long exposures. Compared to yesterday's eclipse, the below photo is missing a couple solar flares that we could just barely see as red spots along the edge of the moon. But this photo does give a sense of the wispy arms of the corona stretching out from the Sun. ABOVE CREDIT: Dennis Di Cicco ABOVE SOURCE: Basic Solar Eclipse Info — Great American Eclipse You've probably seen umpteen million descriptions of eclipses by now, but yes, it really did get dark and noticeably cooler during totality (it actually started cooling down before the Sun was completely blocked). It wasn't quite as dark as night, but more like the mid stages of dusk and dawn. We could make out a couple planets (Venus and Jupiter, I think), though not really any stars. We didn't have a great view of the horizon, and we were all focused on the eclipse itself, anyway, so I didn't notice the 360° sunset that others have mentioned. And I didn't notice any animals doing anything strange, either (though a flock of birds did fly overhead right as totality happened, which was pretty cool). One thing that seems obvious in hindsight is that I should have used sunscreen. Even partially blocked by the moon, staring at the Sun for a couple hours is still a lot of sunlight. A few of us ended up with a bit of a sunburn. Now, to address the overhyping, I've heard some people describe the eclipse as an almost spiritual or transcendent experience. Even Randall Munroe of XKCD fame said "A total eclipse is like someone broke the sky." Yeah, that's going too far. It's a very cool thing to see, but it's not life changing. If there's going to be an eclipse reasonably close by, or if you've got enough money to travel, it's worth seeing a total eclipse at least once in your life. I'd already seen multiple partial eclipses (including an annular eclipse just last year), and they simply don't compare to a total eclipse. But keep your expectations grounded in the fact that all it really means is that you're in a big shadow. A shadow cast by the Moon, but still just a shadow. ETA: I nearly forgot to mention, we also had an assortment of appropriately themed snacks. I had a hard time finding the Moon Pies, so I suspect we were far from the only people who did this.

If tiktaalik evolved into acanthostega, why are there no intermediary forms? Why are there no intermediary forms between any two creatures that one evolved from? This reminds me of an old joke. A creationist complains to a scientist about a gap in the fossil record between an ancient animal and a modern one. The scientist gets lucky and finds a transitional form intermediate between the two. But the creationist just replies, 'Well now you've made the problem even worse. Instead of only one gap, now you have two.' Tiktaalik was only discovered in 2004. At the time, it was heralded as a near-perfect transitional form between fish like Panderichthyes and Eushthenopteron and early tetrapods like Acanthostega and Ichthyostega, and even acquired the nickname of being a 'fishibian'. It seems it didn't take long for creationists to now see two gaps instead of just one. But to actually answer the question, the reason is because fossils are quite rare. When most organisms die, their remains are completely consumed by scavengers and decomposers. It takes a very unique and unlikely set of circumstances to preserve their remains and go through the fossilization process. And then it takes another fortuitous set of circumstances for those fossils to be exposed through erosion, and then found before erosion carries on further and destroys them completely. The fossils we've found only represent a small subset of all the life that has ever existed on this planet. Just for perspective, consider the non-bird dinosaurs. We've only found something like 700 – 1000 non-bird dinosaurs species from their entire 165 million year history. In comparison, there are 6500 named mammal species just in the present, not counting unnamed living species, or the many, many species that have existed in the past and are now extinct. So we know that the actual number of dinosaur species over that entire 165 million year history must have been orders of magnitude higher than the mere 1000 species we've found so far. And it's the same for other groups of organisms. We know that the fossil record is largely incomplete, especially the fossils we've found so far. Some transitions are extremely well documented (like older apes to modern humans). Some remain pretty much entirely undiscovered (like non-flying animals to pterosaurs). But most fall somewhere in between (like fish to tetrapods). As researchers make more and more discoveries, they continue to fill in the gaps in our understanding. And for the time being, at least, this process shows no signs of slowing down. But even though we'll probably never know all of the details, everything we have found points squarely to natural evolutionary processes. Just as a side note, given how incomplete the fossil record is, it's very unlikely that we've found direct ancestor to descendant relationships in most cases. The transitional forms are more like cousins of the actual ancestors. In some cases, we know that certain fossils can't be ancestors because of the timeframes, but that instead they've preserved certain ancestral conditions.

Why do most Americans prefer processed food and artificial over fresh and natural food? Because ‘processing’ isn’t the boogey man you think it is. Processed foods are delicious. And in many cases, the processing actually makes the foods safer and more nutritious. ABOVE SOURCE: The Truth About Eating Processed Foods — The Bodybuilding Dietitians Let me give an example. I like milk and dairy products. Only one time in my life have I I tried unprocessed milk, right after milking it from the cow. It was even still warm. But most of the time, I buy my milk from the grocery store, so I want it pasteurized to make sure it's safe from pathogens. I also like cheese and butter, which are both also processed foods (they're no longer simply raw milk). And for a lot of folks, the processing to make cheese or yogurt can reduce the lactose for people who have issues with that. Same thing with bread. I could eat bread all day. Raw, unprocessed wheat? Not so much. The grinding and cooking even make the nutrients easier to digest. And meat? Now, don't get me wrong. I mean, how does extra chopping or mixing magically make foods unhealthy? I've got the same pet peeves over 'artificial' ingredients. We don't have Star Trek replicators that can create molecules from scratch from energy. Everything we put into our food came from nature at some point. Where do you draw the line between natural and artificial ingredients? And even if you do have some threshold of chemistry that you'll use to designate 'artificial' ingredients, what does that have to do with health or safety? (As an example from medicine, we synthesize acetylsalicylic acid for aspirin, because it actually has less side effects than the naturally occurring salicylic acid found in willow bark that inspired the medicine.) And don't get me started on the silly saying that if you can't pronounce an ingredient, don't eat it. Have you ever seen all the chemical constituents of an egg? Practically all food is a complex mix of lots and lots of hard to pronounce chemicals. Most of those chemicals are safe. Some aren't. But whether or not they're safe has no correlation to how easy they are to pronounce. ABOVE SOURCE: Ingredients of an All-Natural Egg So yeah. I like sausage and bread and ham and pasteurized milk and all types of other processed foods I can buy from the grocery store. I eat processed food because I'm not a wild animal. While I was looking for images for processed foods, I came across many figures where people try to add an extra category, of ‘ultra processed’. Here’s one that was especially silly: ABOVE SOURCE: ABOVE SOURCE: MailOnline's guide to tell ultra-processed food apart They called French fries ultra processed. Sliced potatoes fried in oil. I’m not sure how much less processing you can do to a cooked food. And they’ve got ice cream on there. My family had a hand cranked ice cream maker when I was growing up, and we used it quite a bit for extended family get togethers. It’s just milk, cream, sugar, and a little vanilla, mixed up in a container surrounded by ice and rock salt. What’s ‘ultra processed’ about that? Now, I’m not saying an excess of fries and ice cream would make a healthy diet, but it’s got nothing to do with the amount of processing that went into making them.

If statistics are correct that one in ten men are gay, then which one of the twelve disciples of Christ was gay? One of them had to be a closet case. That’s not how probabilities work. Taking your statistic at face value, the probability that at least one of the 12 disciples was gay would be calculated as: 1 − ( 1 − p ) n 1 − ( 1 – 1 10 ) 12 71.8 % And sure, 71.8% is decently high odds, but it’s not guaranteed that “One of them had to be a closet case.” Take in other potential objections, such as whether or not that stat truly is accurate, or whether folks 2000 years ago even had the same conceptions of gay vs. straight as we do today, and it’s problematic to try to draw any conclusions around this.

Isn't it crazy that 1 man managed to convince billions of people that they evolved from an animal? Actually, yes it is. That's why Darwin is held in such high esteem as the genius he was, and why he was granted the honor of being buried in Westminster Abbey. Other naturalists had proposed ideas of transubstantiation before Charles Darwin, including his grandfather Erasmus Darwin. However, none of those predecessors had managed to convince the larger scientific establishment to take evolution particularly seriously. And Edward Blyth had hit on ideas of natural selection before Darwin published the Origin, though Blyth's comments on the matter went largely unnoticed. Somewhat famously (at least among us nerds), William Wallace also discovered natural selection independently, and even submitted a joint presentation of papers with Darwin to the Linnaean Society of London in 1858. But this submission also didn't have much impact. What did have tremendous impact was when Darwin finally published his book, On the Origin of Species, in 1859. The arguments and evidence he compiled in that book were enormously compelling. Practically overnight, evolution and universal common descent went from a somewhat disreputable position among fringe academics to accepted mainstream science. It was a monumental work on par with the likes of Newton and Einstein. Much of science progresses by incremental contributions from many different researchers. The subsequent history of evolutionary science after Darwin does follow this more general pattern. Looking through the Wikipedia article on the Modern synthesis, you find plenty of contributors like Ernst Mayr, G. Ledyard Stebbins, Theodosius Dobzhansky, E. B. Ford, Bernhard Rensch, Ivan Schmalhausen, George Gaylord Simpson, R. A. Fisher, William Bateson, Julian Huxley, J.B.S. Haldane, and more. But none of those folks, as intelligent as they were, had the same paradigm shifting impact as Charles Darwin. To put it another way, human knowledge had finally progressed to the point where discovering evolution was practically inevitable. It would have happened eventually. But without Darwin, it would have been a more prolonged process that would have taken a bit longer, and the folks who contributed would probably still be mentioned in the history books, but they wouldn't be household names (just look to Alfred Wegener and continental drift). Darwin was a true genius, with a monumental impact on biology. So yes, it is always a bit crazy when you come across such singular geniuses.

ABOVE SOURCE: Synoptic Gospels - Wikipedia Anyway, back when I was a Christian, I was convinced that I could feel God's presence when I prayed. Now, even at the time, I knew in the back of my mind that such a warm fuzzy feeling wasn't overwhelming proof and could have been due to more Earthly causes, but I did my best to suppress such thoughts and take that sensation as proof of God's existence. But as I began questioning my religion for other reasons, I allowed myself to question the authenticity of this feeling, as well, and eventually realized that I'd merely conditioned myself to generate this feeling on my own. In fact, I'd gotten so good at it, that I can still do it on demand. Or to put it another way, many of us who are atheists now did pray to God to show that he exists. Some of us, like me, did experience a warm-fuzzy feeling that we took as proof. Others never felt anything at all. But now, I can safely say, I don't think any of us (or anyone else, for that matter), ever experienced anything that was actually divine.

What's your go-to healthy snack when cravings hit? Single serve bags of potato chips: Because let's be frank. When it's an honest to goodness craving, rabbit food just isn't going to cut it. I see a bunch of other answers here trying to promote 'healthy' snacks, and while all those would be fine under normal circumstances when you’re merely peckish, they're just not going to satisfy a craving the same way junk food will. And I've tried. You eat the healthy alternative, and you're not satiated. You just want more. And if you eat enough until you're full, you've just eaten more calories without actually satisfying the craving. But a single serve bag of potato chips is only 1 oz of food, and only 160 calories. Sure, it's not the best thing to eat all the time. But every once in a while? That's not going to kill you. And it will actually satisfy your craving with all that starchy, greasy, salty goodness. And the fact that it's in a single serving bag makes portion control that much easier. With a full size bag, it's easy to just keep going back for one more chip, one more chip, one more chip, until eventually you've eaten a lot more than you should have. But if you know the one small bag is all you get, you eat your one serving and stop. The whole point is that a healthy diet is all about balance and moderation. And abstinence will just lead to worse cravings, or even falling off the healthy diet altogether. No single food in moderation is going to be all that bad for you. Just make sure to balance it out with enough other types of food to have a healthy diet overall. On days when the cravings aren't quite so bad to give in to potato chips, my next go-tos are pickles and olives (or olive salad on crackers). You still get enough saltiness to help satisfy the craving (and the olive oil from the olives), but not too terrible on the calories. After that is probably pita chips. Still starchy and salty, but not quite as greasy as the chips.

Do you know any heterosexual males who have absolutely zero interest in sports, and couldn’t care less about the Super Bowl, the World Series, the NBA Playoffs or the World Cup? Not in real life, no. I see a lot of men speaking up here on Quora to say that they have absolutely zero interest in sports, and I believe them. But I also think they're outliers, and it's only because Quora has such a huge user base that there are so many answers here making that point. In real life, every guy I know has at least some minimum level of interest in at least some sports. The most casual, even if they don't particularly keep up with any sports throughout the regular seasons or playoffs, usually at least want to watch either the Super Bowl or the World Cup finals, or will sit down to watch a game if they're with somebody who is a big fan. Perhaps part of that is the social side of things, but at Super Bowl parties, they're right there on the couch intently watching the game along with all the other guys. Some women, on the other hand, when they say they have zero interest in sports, really do seem to have zero interest. Even when they show up to a Super Bowl party, they'll wander out of the room with the game on to go talk to other women with no interest in the game. I'm not going to wade into the debate on whether this is cultural conditioning or something innate, but pretty much every guy I know in real life has at least some interest in sports, and many guys take it very seriously. FWIW, I fall somewhere in the middle. I played a decent amount of sports growing up, and I know the basic rules for all the major U.S. sports (even back to the now defunct two line pass in hockey). I do watch games from some of the major sports leagues, but often with the TV on in the background while I go about other chores, not sitting there intently throughout the whole game. Even for the Steelers, I'll only sit down for the whole game if I don't have anything more important going on. And as one more side note, after having just watched the Summer Olympics, I’ll add that sport climbing is hella impressive (men’s and women’s). Those athletes accomplish feats that seem practically impossible.

Why has Quora devolved into a toxic cesspool? For just about any question that starts with, "Why has Quora...", the answer is almost always money. I didn't get started on Quora back at the very beginning, but I still got on early enough to get a taste of what it was at its best. I mean, you still got people like Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton contributing answers when I first started using the site. But as great as Quora was back then, it was operating at a loss. It was living off of the cash from investors, trying to build up its userbase and reputation so that it would eventually become profitable. Those investors weren't putting their money into Quora just for fun. They want to see a return on their investment. And operating a social media site is expensive. Googling it just now, it has something like 400 million active monthly users. That takes tons of hardware and bandwidth, which costs tons of money. So, if Quora wants to start turning a profit, they have to find ways to reduce costs and increase the things that bring in money. And bringing in money mostly boils down to advertising, which means getting people to 'engage' with the platform. So, the questions Quora's management asks aren't how changes will affect the user experience, but how they'll affect the bottom line. And cutting down on moderation is an easy way to cut costs. Can a negative user experience drive some people away from the site? Sure. But you're still here asking questions, and I'm still here answering them. And according to Semrush.com, it looks like Quora's traffic has just continued growing over the past 6 months, despite all of us users complaining about the decline in the user experience (accessing stats going beyond 6 months cost money that I'm not going to spend just to answer this question): In short, the user experience on Quora has declined because it saves Quora money by not having to pay as much for moderation, while it doesn’t seem to have had a big impact on the engagement which brings in the ad revenue.

Are beneficial mutations rare? Yes. Beneficial mutations are rare. While I've never been able to find actual numbers specifying just how rare beneficial mutations are in comparison to deleterious or neutral mutations (admittedly, I'm not an expert on this), I have found plenty of general statements from technical and/or reputable sources about beneficial mutations being rare, along with one calculation I found that implied they were basically negligible in comparison to neutral or deleterious mutations. I actually spent a decent amount of time researching this for one particular debate in the comments section of another of my answers*, so I'll share a bit of what I found then, along with another paper I just found recently. Like I said, most of what I found was broad or general statements in those sources, especially in the background sections or in general discussion. So here are the links to those sources along with excerpts of what the authors stated. In each case, the bolding was done by me, to highlight the most relevant statements. The Effects of Deleterious Mutations on Evolution at Linked Sites Brian Charlesworth MUTATIONS that increase the fitness of their carriers are, of course, the basis of adaptive evolution. For this reason, the literature on evolutionary genetics is full of studies that document “positive” selection on genetic variants in natural populations—with the advent of data on the resequencing of numerous whole genomes from the same species, we can expect a tidal wave of such examples. But, as was pointed out long ago by geneticists such as Timofeeff-Ressovsky (1940) and Muller (1949, 1950), most mutations that affect the phenotype must be deleterious, because biological machinery has been subject to billions of years of selection to improve its performance. Because the nucleotide sites at which deleterious mutations can arise are numerous and distributed throughout the genome, the constant mutational production of deleterious variants and their elimination by “purifying” selection have major effects on the mean fitness of a population, its level of inbreeding depression, and its genetic variability with respect to fitness components. The population genetics of beneficial mutations H. Allen Orr The history of population genetics, especially theoretical population genetics, presents a paradox. Although population genetics arose from the fusion of Darwin's theory of adaptation by natural selection with Mendel's theory of inheritance, the field has been concerned historically far more with deleterious and, later, with neutral mutations than with beneficial ones. The paradox has, of course, a simple solution: population geneticists were looking under the lamp post. In particular, mutations having negative or negligible effects on fitness are more common and thus easily studied, while those having positive effects on fitness are far rarer and thus studied only with difficulty. Genetic Mutation Laurence Loewe A single mutation can have a large effect, but in many cases, evolutionary change is based on the accumulation of many mutations with small effects. Mutational effects can be beneficial, harmful, or neutral, depending on their context or location. Most non-neutral mutations are deleterious. In general, the more base pairs that are affected by a mutation, the larger the effect of the mutation, and the larger the mutation's probability of being deleterious. Neutral Theory: The Null Hypothesis of Molecular Evolution Laurent Duret It must be stressed that the neutral theory of molecular evolution is not an anti-Darwinian theory. Both the selectionist and neutral theories recognize that natural selection is responsible for the adaptation of organisms to their environment. Both also recognize that most new mutations in functionally important regions are deleterious and that purifying selection quickly removes these deleterious mutations from populations. Thus, these mutations do not contribute—or contribute very little—to sequence divergence between species and to polymorphisms within species. Rather, the dispute between selectionists and neutralists relates only to the relative proportion of neutral and advantageous mutations that contribute to sequence divergence and polymorphism. Revisiting the genetic load argument with Dan Graur Laurence A. Moran The most difficult part of these calculations is estimating the percentage of mutations that are beneficial, neutral, and deleterious. Population geneticists have rightly assumed that the number of beneficial (selected) mutations is insignificant so they concentrate on the number of deleterious mutations. The estimates range from about 4% of the total mutations to about 40% of the total based on the analysis of mutations in coding regions. I even found one paper that calculated the fraction of deleterious mutations as 1 – fo, where fo is the fraction of neutral mutations. In other words, beneficial mutations were so rare that they were considered negligible and didn't even enter into the calculation. So, I know that doesn't do a great job quantifying it, other than to say that beneficial mutations are much more rare than neutral or deleterious mutations. * The answer with that debate in the comments section was Jeff Lewis's answer to How does an evolution denier explain the different covid-19 variants that have emerged?

How do you feel about reviving characters from the dead in books? Not in a zombie way. I feel that it reduces the stakes and the tension in stories, especially if it's an ongoing series or serial, or happens early in a standalone story. Part of what makes death so profound and tragic is its finality. You no longer exist, and you will never again exist in the future. But when a story shows characters being revived from death, the stakes are dramatically reduced. Death is no longer necessarily final. You know that the writers can always pull some trick to bring any character back, so whenever somebody dies, you're never quite sure if they're really dead dead, or merely mostly dead. It's similar with a related theme of showing characters living in an afterlife, especially depending on how the afterlife is portrayed. In real life, even among folks who profess a belief in an afterlife, there's no way to be absolutely sure until you die yourself, and so there's always some level of doubt, and the possibility that us materialists might be right, after all. But in stories where an immortal afterlife is portrayed and becomes a certainty in that universe, then once again, death loses its sting. The character's not really gone. They've essentially moved, and the other characters just have to wait a while before they get to visit them again. That's not to say you can't still have good stories featuring 'resurrections' and afterlives. I already hinted at one with my 'mostly dead' comment. The Princess Bride was a great movie*. But you have to admit, that reviving Westley really set the tone for the remainder of the movie. It removed any doubt that the heroes would all somehow still be alive at the end. Coco was another great movie, this time showing folks existing in the afterlife. But, it was shown early on that this afterlife wasn't necessarily eternal, and you might still 'die' a second death – establishing real stakes. Also, when Abuelita died at the end, it wasn't really all that sad of a moment, because you knew she'd 'survive' in the Land of the Dead for a few more generations, at least. And as one final example, Star Trek Lower Decks has killed and then resurrected a few characters. But the whole point of doing it in this series was as parody, poking fun of the way the more serious Star Trek series have been so cavalier about resurrecting dead characters. So sure, you can still have good stories featuring resurrections or afterlives, but they have to be handled appropriately. At the very least, such stories reduce the stakes and tension around ordinary deaths, so the story writers need to find other ways to compensate, or just recognize that it's not a story dealing with such high stakes. *Yeah, I know most of my examples were movies instead of books, but it’s still general storytelling.

Is the Fahrenheit temperature scale calibrated so that 0 or 100 are meaningful (to something other than water)? In a paper that Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit submitted to the Royal Society, he explained for himself the three points originally used to calibrate his thermometers (though in principle, only two points should have been required). If you can read Latin, the full paper is available here: Otherwise, you can find an English translation of a relevant portion here: Here is how he defined each point: The first is found in the uncalibrated part or the beginning of the scale, and is determined by a mixture of ice, water and ammonium chloride or even sea salt. If the thermometer is placed in this mixture, its liquid descends as far as the degree that is marked with a zero. The second point is obtained if water and ice are mixed without the aforementioned salts. When the thermometer is placed in this mixture, its liquid reaches the 32nd degree. I call this ‘freezing point’. The third point is situated at the 96th degree. Alcohol expands up to this point when it is held in the mouth or under the armpit of a living man in good health until it has completely acquired his body heat. So, zero was the lowest temperature easily achievable in a lab, with just water, ice, and salt. The upper point of human body temperature was set at 96°, which for people already used to traditional measurements is a nice, even eight dozen. From there, it seems that Anders Celsius's work had a major influence to use the freezing and boiling points of water (at standard pressure) as the main calibration points. So using the already defined 32° for the freezing point of pure water, Fahrenheit's scale was tweaked just a bit to make the boiling point 212°, which meant a nice round 180° between them (or a half circle's worth of degrees). By the way, that tweak undid his 0° calibration point. In the modern day Fahrenheit scale, that brine solution sits at 4°F. So, it was a bit of a meandering development, but there was some rationale for the original calibration points. At least Fahrenheit set cold temperatures as the lower values, unlike Mr. Celsius who originally set his scale with boiling at 0° and freezing at 100°.

Why is the Francesinha the world's best sandwich? This question contains a fallacy, and so it can’t be answered as asked. Now, I’d never heard of the Francesinha before coming across this question. So if you’re like me and had similarly never heard of it, here’s what this dish looks like: And admittedly, that does look pretty darn good. But I’m also not going to call it a sandwich. Sandwiches are meant to be eaten with your hands. That’s kind of the whole point from the very earliest times when the Earl of Sandwich invented them. If you need a knife and a fork to eat a food, that’s not a sandwich. I mean, you could put your bacon in between your French toast, but that wouldn’t make it a sandwich. So however good a Francesinha might taste, it can’t take the title for world’s best sandwich*. So what is the best sandwich? Man, there are just way too many choices to narrow it down to one. You’ve got everything from hoagies to BLTs to Reubens to club sandwiches to Bánh mì to panini to tortas to cheesesteaks to Primanti’s and on and on and on. Heck, on a cold day after playing out in the snow, a simple grilled cheese with a bowl of tomato soup can’t be beat. If you have a Bible at hand, can you open it up to a random page and see what it says? Maybe it will change your life. Okay. I decided to give this a try, and I really did open up to random pages rather than cherry picking verses that I knew were problematic just to make a point. And to up the odds that I’d get something good, I actually tried it three times, not just once. Here’s what I got: First Attempt – Joshua 14 and Joshua 15 Well, there's nothing really profound or life changing here. It was mostly just details of how the conquered areas of the Promised Land were divied out to the various Jewish people. Just to give a taste of how tedious it is: And their south boundary ran from the end of the Dead Sea, from the bay that faces southward; it goes out southward of the ascent of Akrabbim, passes along to Zin, and goes up south of Kadesh-barnea, along by Hezron, up to Addar, makes a turn to Karka, passes along to Azmon, goes out by the Wadi of Egypt, and comes to its end at the sea. This shall be your south boundary. If you wanted to be less charitable, you could point out that the Israelites were the evil conquerors who went in and subjugated or displaced the people already living there, but that kind of thing is so common throughout history that it's just par for the course. I mean, look at how many times the lands that would become England were invaded and conquered by outsiders, or basically the entire history of Rome. (Also, somewhat thankfully, these stories about conquering the Promised Land probably aren’t true – Frans du Plessis's answer to Do we have extra-biblical evidence for the origins of the Israelites?) Second Attempt – 2 Chronicles 1 and 2 Chronicles 2 Well, at least we get one of the classic Bible stories, here, with God offering Solomon anything he wanted, and Solomon asking for wisdom. But it all reads as just typical ancient literature, so still nothing life changing. I'll note the the final couple verses, though: Then Solomon took a census of all the aliens who were residing in the land of Israel, after the census that his father David had taken, and there were found to be one hundred fifty-three thousand six hundred. Seventy thousand of them he assigned as laborers, eighty thousand as stonecutters in the hill country, and three thousand six hundred as overseers to make the people work. Huh. No calls to send them back across the border where they came from, or complaints that the immigrants were stealing Israelite jobs. Just a pragmatic approach of putting them to work. I feel like there might be a lesson there for certain modern day folks who claim to follow the Bible. Third Attempt – Job 30 and Job 31 These were the chapters where Job wrapped up his defense to his friends who insisted that he must have done something wrong to have incurred God's wrath, while Job insisted that he'd done nothing wrong and had lived a good life. It's really just a reminder of how unfair and cruel God can be. As I've said elsewhere, the lesson one takes away from Job is that might makes right, and God is the mightiest of all. So I actually gave it three shots. None of the chapters I came across offered anything particularly profound or life changing. And actually, that is an important point that I don't think a lot of folks really understand. You so often hear people say that, even if you're not religious, at least the Bible is great literature, or carries profound moral lessons. But on the whole, it isn't, really. There may be certain sections of the Bible that are good (e.g. Ecclesiastes). But when you look at the entire Bible, it's a very mixed bag, with the tedious and mundane parts outnumbering the good parts.

What is the probability that a satellite the size of the moon, would orbit just the right distance from a planet the size of the earth, that from the planet, it appears the same size as a star the size of the sun, at its distance from that planet? The Milky Way contains somewhere between 100 billion and 400 billion stars, and probably at least that many planets. I’m sure there are interesting coincidences of some sort or another in practically all solar systems. On our planet, it happens to be a moon that appears to be roughly the same size in the sky as the Sun. On other planets, there are probably different coincidences that we don’t enjoy here. On the other hand, I’ve seen claims like this one from NASA, that “The Moon makes Earth a more livable planet by moderating our home planet's wobble on its axis, leading to a relatively stable climate. It also causes tides, creating a rhythm that has guided humans for thousands of years.” So if large moons like ours are necessary for the development of civilization, then that leads to a bit of survivorship bias. The only planets with intelligent life with the scientific knowledge to ponder such things would be planets with large moons. Other planets without large moons, even if they had life, wouldn’t have stable enough climates to make civilizations possible. In other words, our planet having a large moon isn’t so much a coincidence, as it was a pre-condition for us to develop in the first place.

If in the USA we have freedom of press, why is it legal for social media to control what we can and can not post? Quite simply, the servers hosting social media are private property, owned (or at least leased/rented) by the social media companies. Just like you have control over your own property, and can tell me what types of signs or billboards I'm allowed to post on your yard, social media companies have control over their property, and can tell people what they're allowed to post on their servers. I'm perfectly free to post whatever signs or billboards I want on my own yard (within zoning restrictions at least). Likewise, if you want to spend the money for your own website, you're free to post whatever you want there. But what you're asking for is to ignore the private property rights of the companies that own the servers hosting social media, and to give you special concessions to infringe upon those companies' property rights. Why are Americans and Middle Easterners generally still obsessed with religion while Europeans consider it a private matter and limit public discussion? What caused Europeans to become more atheist while the other two did not? Imagine if you saw someone on the highway, driving full speed towards a bridge that had just collapsed, so recently that there weren't yet any cops or warning signs. Would you try to get their attention to get them to slow down? Or would you consider that to be too pushy and rude, and leave them on their way to hopefully notice on their own that the bridge was out in time? Now, I'm an atheist myself, but I can certainly understand the mindset of Christians wanting to share their faith. I mean, they sincerely believe it. They honestly think that people who aren't Christians risk an eternity of torture. It doesn't matter if you want to be clever and say such a God is evil and not worthy of worship. In their mind, that God is the reality, and clever word games will just land you in Hell. So yeah, they're going to be pretty vocal about trying to convince other people to see the light. What would you expect them to do? Be polite? Smile and wave as you go hurtling down that highway towards the collapsed bridge? Of course, in a multicultural society, there's a delicate balance of trying to help others vs. live and let live. I have plenty of Christian friends, and we will occasionally have discussions about religion, but we never get too pushy about it. Still, I'm always a bit baffled by the folks who wonder why sincere Christians try spread the Gospels. They're telling the truth when they say they believe in it all. What type of psychopath could just sit idly by and watch people doom themselves to such a horrible fate?

What do you do when your kid says that they are sick but you think they are faking it? I was pretty lucky growing up, in that I think my mom had hated school just as much as I did. So she was pretty lenient about letting me stay home "sick". To be fair, I never completely faked it, but I did embellish and play up minor headaches that I wouldn't even think twice about as an adult and still going to work. So, I tried to extend the same courtesy to my own daughter when she was still at home and in school. As long as she kept up with all her schoolwork and still got good grades (which she always did – to brag just a bit, she graduated as salutatorian*), I never pried too much into just how "sick" she really was. If she wanted to stay home for the day every once in a while, I let her. *Technically, I was a valedictorian, myself, but our school didn't do weighted averages or anything else to break the tie. I don't remember the exact number, anymore, but we had something like 20 valedictorians – not exactly super prestigious.
